sentences.text: Giraffatitan is a genus of sauropod dinosaur, a name meaning "titanic giraffe".
Currently, only one species is known: Giraffatitan brancai.
From 1914 until the 1990s, this animal was considered the largest known dinosaur.
However, recent discoveries suggest that giant titanosaurians may have surpassed it in sheer mass.
The species was originally described by Werner Janensch in 1914.
Its fossils were discovered in the Tendaguru Formation.
The species name brancai honors the German paleontologist Wilhelm von Branca.
The genus Giraffatitan was established by Friedrich von Huene in 1988, though the text attributes the authority to Paul, 1988.
The current scientific consensus is that Giraffatitan was a fully terrestrial animal.
Teeth wear in the specimen suggests it bit and tore plant matter rather than grinding it, indicating the absence of a trunk.
Studies by Lawrence Witmer in 2001 suggest that despite high skull openings, the nostrils were located near the tip of the snout.
Nevertheless, the exact placement of fleshy nostrils is debated, with researchers hypothesizing as many as five possible locations.
Glycogen bodies are considered a more likely explanation for the sacral enlargement than a "second brain".
Giraffatitan brancai was originally classified as the species Brachiosaurus brancai.
George Olshevsky elevated Giraffatitan to full genus status in 1991.
In 1929, Janensch assigned Brachiosaurus species to the subfamily Brachiosaurinae within the family Bothrosauropodidae.
Giraffatitan lived between 145 and 150 million years ago during the Late Jurassic.
It lived during the late Jurassic Period, specifically the Kimmeridgian to Tithonian stages.
Fossils have been found in what is now the Lindi Region of Tanzania.
The animal lived in what is now Tanzania during the Late Jurassic.
In 1988, Gregory S. Paul suggested separating the species based on differences in vertebral proportions compared to B. altithorax.
Gregory S. Paul initially proposed separating the species only at the subgenus level rather than the genus level.
Daniel Chure rejected the separation in 2010, but most subsequent studies from 2012 onwards accepted the name Giraffatitan.
